processing: Mature leaf made into dark raw tea with pile fermentation, then steamed and pressed into rectangular bricks and dried. Today it is mostly met as green brick (qing zhuan) and rice brick (mi zhuan).
harvest_season: Not sold by picking date. As with other border brick teas, the leaf is mature and gathered through the growing season, so the pressing year matters more than the harvest.
appearance_dry: A hard rectangular brick, dark green-brown in the green brick style, often carrying the 川 mark.
appearance_liquor: Orange-red and clear in aged green brick, deeper red in rice brick.
appearance_wet: Coarse dark brown leaf and stem fragments, as usual for brick tea.
taste_profile: Coarse but not rough, mature but not thin, with an aged aroma and a lasting finish in older bricks. Age can bring a nutty, almond-like note.

brewing.notes: Chip off a piece with a tea knife and rinse once. Boiling water always; simmering it in a pot brings out more sweetness, and it holds up to milk.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year, as a whole brick, under names such as Zhaoliqiao's 川 brand and other Chibi makers. Young bricks are drinkable, but people pay more for aged ones, whose liquor goes amber and red. Check the factory and date, since the place name is used loosely across the Chibi area.
description:
This is the old name behind Hubei brick tea. Yangloudong is a small town in Chibi where the Mufu Mountains meet the Jianghan Plain, and its bricks, known simply as Dong Cha, travelled north along the Tea Road. Today people usually buy it as qing zhuan, green brick, which despite the name is a dark tea.

The leaf is mature and is fermented in piles before steaming and pressing, as with other dark teas meant for the border trade. Pressing made the tea easy to carry over long distances, and it also gives a slow, even kind of ageing.

The character it is praised for is summed up in a local phrase: coarse but not rough, old but not thin. Expect orange-red liquor from an older brick, a settled aged scent and a long finish, sometimes with a hint of almond. Most mistakes come from water that is too cool; this tea wants a full boil.

When buying, the 川 mark is the name to know, but Chibi has several makers and the Yangloudong label is used broadly. Ask for the factory and pressing year, and avoid bricks that smell musty.
history:
Tea growing around Yangloudong is often traced to the Tang, though that claim comes from general accounts. Firmer ground is the Qianlong period, when Shanxi merchants opened firms such as San Yu Chuan and Ju Sheng Chuan, making cap-shaped bundled tea and later rectangular bricks. A 川 stamped on the bricks became a mark Mongolian herders trusted, according to local accounts. A news report dates the first green brick to 1843, a date other accounts do not repeat.

In the Xianfeng and Tongzhi years, Russian, German and Japanese firms, along with traders from Hankou, Tianjin and Guangzhou, set up in the town. After 1949 its factories were merged into a state brick tea plant, which moved to nearby Zhaoliqiao in 1953, and the tradition continued under that name.
